chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: [The scene shows the front of MEDEA'S house in Corinth. A road on the right leads to the royal palace, one on the left to the harbor. The NURSE is alone on stage. The CHILDREN and their ATTENDANT enter.]

NURSE. If only the Argo had never spread its wings across the sea to Colchis through the dark Symplegades. If only no pine had ever been split in the glens of Pelion to shape that first oar in the hands of brave men, who sailed to win the All-Golden Fleece for King Pelias. Then my own princess, Medea, her heart torn open by love for Jason, would never have sailed to the towered shores of old Iolcus. The daughters of King Pelias, deceived, would never have spilled their father's blood. She would never have fled in terror, hunted for that fierce sin, here to Corinth with Jason and her children. The people of this country welcomed her in her need, and she, in word and deed, served Jason faithfully. Surely this is what holds humanity together through every dark day — when husband and wife move in one music. But now the world is bitter, and true love sickens like a poisoned thing. Jason has abandoned my mistress and his own two sons to make his bed in a king's chamber. He is taking a new wife: Creon's daughter, who now is head and chief of Corinth. Betrayed to the bone, Medea cries out the oath the two of them swore, calls back the clasped hands, the pledge that words cannot describe, and begs God in heaven to witness the end — to see how Jason has paid his debt. She has been fasting, cold, her body given over to pain, her days wasted in weeping, ever since she learned he was false. Her eyes never lift; her face stays in the dust. If friends try to speak to her, she hears no more than a dead rock or a wave breaking on the shore. Only the white throat sometimes writhes in sudden shame, and alone she moans the names of her father, her country, her home — all of it abandoned for the sake of this man who is throwing her away. Now, locked out from any home — alas, she knows now how rare a thing that was. I think she dreads, rather than welcomes, the sight of her children near her. That is what makes me tremble most: that she may do — I don't know what. Her heart is no light thing; it does not bear injury well. I know that woman, yes, and I am afraid of her. Will she creep alone into that old room where Jason's bed still lies, and bleed to death? She has a sharpened blade for it. Or will she kill the bridegroom and the king, and bring some worse thing on herself? She is a fierce spirit. Few, I think, will rouse her hatred and walk away unhurt; she is not easily humbled. Ah! Here come the children back from their games, rested and happy, with no thought of their mother's pain. Young lives always turn away from gloom.

ATTENDANT. Old treasure of my lady's chamber, what are you doing out here alone before the gates, muttering to yourself about old troubles? Will our mistress really be content to be left so long without you?

NURSE. Grey guardian of Jason's children — a good slave has griefs of her own when something hurts the master's house. Yes, it grips the heart. I have wandered so deep into dark dreams I longed to come out here alone and cry Medea's wrongs to the silent Earth and Sky.
ATTENDANT. What — are the tears still running in her eyes?
NURSE. I wish I could be like you, untroubled. Her sorrow is barely awake yet — not half its dangers grown. [He moves toward the house, but the NURSE stops him.]
ATTENDANT. Poor mad spirit — if a man may say so of mad mistresses. And nothing yet has reached her ears about her latest reason for tears.
NURSE. What reason, old man? Don't keep one word from me.
ATTENDANT. It's nothing. Better to forget what you've heard.
NURSE. No, friend, by your beard — don't hide it from me. I will keep silent if you ask.

ATTENDANT. I overheard an old man talking, where he sat at draughts in the sun beside the fountain gate, and never noticed me standing nearby. He said it is Creon's will — Creon being lord of all this land — that she be sent away to exile, with both her sons. Maybe it's all false. I know no more, and I wish it weren't true.
NURSE. Jason will never stand for it — his own sons exiled — however hot his rage runs against their mother.
ATTENDANT. They say old love burns low when new love wakes. He is no longer husband or father here, no kin to anyone in this house.
NURSE. Then this is ruin. New waves breaking in to wreck us before we have righted ourselves from the old.
ATTENDANT. Hold your tongue. Our mistress will be told in good time. Don't say a word about it.
NURSE. My babies — what do you think of your father's love? God curse him, no — he is still my master. But oh, to those who loved him, he is a poor friend.

ATTENDANT. And what man on earth is any different? Have you lived this long without learning that every man loves his own head better than other men's? He is dreaming of his new bride's bed and giving no thought to his sons. [The CHILDREN and the ATTENDANT go inside.]

NURSE. Go on, run inside, my little ones. All will end happily. Keep them apart from her. Do not let their mother see them while her heart is dark. Last night I saw a flame standing in her eye, as though she hated them and wanted — I do not know what. Her wrath will never turn or sleep until she has — Go in. And if some must suffer, may it be not us who love her, but some enemy. VOICE [within]. Oh shame and pain — oh, woe is me. I wish I could die in my misery.

NURSE. Listen, children — she stirs again, her frozen heart, her sleeping wrath. Inside, quick. Don't cross her path. Don't rouse that dark eye in its pain — that fierce sea-spirit, that wellspring of a will untaught and unbowed. Quick, now. This weeping cloud has thunder-fire in its heart, slowly gathering, and it must flash before long. I do not know how, for ill or for good, this ungovernable, storm-driven spirit, blind with wrong, will turn. VOICE [within]. Have I not suffered enough? Does it call up no tears? — Ha, you children there beside the wall, fatherless now, may God hate you as I am hated, and your father with you, and this whole house. [As these last words are spoken, the LEADER of the Chorus enters. Other women follow her.]

NURSE. For pity's sake — what have these babies done? What have they to do with their father's sin? Why call your curse on them? Ah, children, all these days my heart bleeds for you. The wills of princes are rough things — always prevailing, seldom crossed, their moods tossed on shifting winds. It is best for ordinary people to walk the level way. Let the long summers find me crowned not with glory but with peace, for gentleness — even her sound is magic, and her ways are wholesome. But the fiercely great have little music on their road, and when the hand of God moves against them, they fall most deep and desolate.

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: LEADER. I heard a voice and a cry, a voice from the eastern seas. Has she still found no peace? Speak, old woman. I stood far off at the gate, and from within came a wailing, a desolate cry. There is no joy left in me — only the griefs of this house, and the love for her that has grown in me.

NURSE. There is no house anymore — it is gone. Her lord seeks a prouder bed, and she wastes in her chamber, not one word of care or kindness will she hear. VOICE [within]. O Zeus, O Earth, O Light — will the fire not stab my brain? What good is living? Will I not lift this slow yoke and let life go, like a beast out in the night, to lie down and be done with pain?

CHORUS. Some Women. A. "O Zeus, O Earth, O Light" — did you hear that cry of an abandoned bride, the wailing for joy that is gone? B. Why do you torment yourself today, wild heart, longing for that hated bed, the cold bed in the earth? Death comes whether or not a person prays for it — uncrowned, unadored. Do not call him to you. C. If another woman lies now where you used to lie, the sin is on his head. Do not tear your face. D. All that you suffer, God sees. Do not waste yourself or weep so bitterly for the breast that was once yours. VOICE [within]. Virgin of Righteousness, Virgin of sacred Troth — you watched when I bound him with an oath. Watch now how that oath ends. Let me see him and his bride, who came after my grief when I had done her no wrong, broken in misery — they and all her house. O God — my mother's home, and the dim shore I left for him, and the voice of my brother's blood.
NURSE. Oh, wild words. Did you hear her cry out to those who guard the faith men have sworn — Themis and Zeus? This new-born rage will work madness before it dies down.

OTHER WOMEN. A. If only she would come out and find our faces — we love her well — and take into her heart the spell of speaking words. B. Alas for the heavy hatred, the anger that keeps on burning. If only it would lessen now — God, I love her still — and surely my love will not fail her here. C. Go — lead her out of that gloomy chamber into the daylight, and tell her, oh, tell her that we love her dearly. D. Go, before her hand falls hard on the innocent. Oh, let be — her grief is moving toward us like an angry sea. [The NURSE goes into the house.]

NURSE. I will go — though what words of mine, what love, will move her? Let them lie with the old lost labors. And yet her eye — do you know the eyes of wild cattle, the lion flash that guards their young? That is how she looks now, if any servant speaks comfort or comes near her at all when she is in this dark mood.

A WOMAN. Alas, the bold cheerful poets of old made all their music for joy, for feasts and dancing, so that Life could listen and be glad. But the darkness and the wrong, the sudden deaths and the dim heart-aching things — will no one ease them with a song, with the music of a thousand strings? Then song would have served us in our need. What good is it, when the banquet is roaring, to add one more lingering cry that no one will hear? They have eaten their fill — all is well. [During the last words MEDEA has come out from the house.]

OTHERS. I heard a song, but it has stopped. Where the tears ran over, a keen cry, but tired, tired — a woman's cry for her heart's desired, for a traitor's kiss and a lost lover. But a prayer, I think, still rises bitterly to God, to Faith, God's ancient daughter — the Faith that drew her over the sundering seas to Hellas, when the midnight breeze shivered and the door of the salt unsounded water closed behind her.

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: MEDEA. Women of Corinth, I have come out so you can see my face — I would not have you despise me. I know that some heads stand high and never falter, even at night, alone — let alone in plain sight of men. And the rest of us, who do not measure each step but feel and cry out — oh, we are drifting, evil things. For what truth is there in men's eyes, that search no heart but in a flash despise a strange face, recoiling from someone who has never wronged them? I know — strangers anywhere must bow themselves and be gentle. Even a Greek wins no praise if he always pursues his own will without regard for others. But this thing — this unimagined blow falling on me out of the sky — has emptied my soul. I dazzle where I stand, the cup of all my life shattered in my hand, longing to die. O my friends — he, the very man whom to know well was the whole world to me, the man I loved — has shown himself most evil. Of all things on earth that bleed and grow, woman is the most bruised herb. We must pay our hoard of gold, saved up for that one day, to buy ourselves a man's love — and what they bring us is a master of our flesh. There begins the whole shame. Then the gamble — for good or ill — what kind of master will he be? She cannot refuse him; and if he so much as hesitates in his courtship, every day of her life is shamed. Thrown into new laws, a new home — she would need magic, or prophecy (no one taught her these things at home) to know how best to manage this thing that sleeps at her side. And the woman who, after long labor, finds some way to make her husband bear with her without straining the yoke too fiercely — blessed is the breath that woman draws. Otherwise, let her pray for death. Her lord, if he gets bored of the face inside the house, goes out — some merrier place will ease his heart. But she waits, her whole vision chained to a single soul. And then, forsooth, they tell us they are the ones who face the call of war while we sit sheltered, hidden from all peril. False mockery. I would rather stand three times to face their battles, shield in hand, than bear one child. But peace — your story and mine cannot be the same. You have this city, your father's home, the joy of friends, hope for the days to come. But I, with no city, am cast aside by the man who married me, a foreign bride won in distant seas and abandoned — no mother near me, no brother, no kin anywhere to take me in out of this storm. So I ask one thing of you. If chance opens some path for me, if my hand can yet find strength to pay Jason back for his sin — do not betray me. In all things else, I know how full of fears a woman is, how faint at need, how she shrinks from the light of battle. But once rob her of her right in a man's love, and there is no bloodier spirit between heaven and hell — I warn you well.

LEADER. I will not betray you. It is just that you strike him. As for those weeping in the dust, those storm-tears — how could I blame them? Wait — Creon, lord of Corinth, is making his way here, and I think he carries some weighty word. [Enter from the right CREON, the King, with armed Attendants.]

CREON. You — sullen-eyed woman, hot with hate against your lord — Medea, I command you here: you and your two children leave this land. Go into exile. Make no delay. I myself, the King, have come today in person to see this charge carried out. I shall not turn homeward until I have led the two children and you beyond the last border of my realm.

MEDEA. Lost — I am lost. My enemies are at the helm, sails flying, in pursuit, and there is no beach, no shore for us in the endless waters. And yet, struck as I am, I will still ask you — for what crime, for what unlawful thing, will you cast me out, O King?

CREON. What crime? I fear you, woman — there is no need to disguise my reasons — I am afraid you will work some dark deed against my child. There are reasons enough for that fear. You come here a known witch, full of strange knowledge in the arts of evil. Your heart is sore at being torn from your lover's arms. And worse, you have made threats — so the alarms have just now reached my ear — against the bride and the groom, and the man who gave the bride, vowing your vengeance. I am sweeping all of that aside before it is too late. I choose to earn your hate now, deliberately, rather than soften with mercy and weep tears of blood later on.

MEDEA. This is not the first or second time, O King, that my reputation has hurt me, has nearly brought me to ruin. How can any man with healthy eyes try to raise his children to be wiser than the rest of men? It only brings them helplessness in the common arts of life and deep envy in their fellow citizens' hearts — that is all their learning earns them. Bring fools knowledge of new things and they call it vanity, not knowledge. And men who used to be honored for their wisdom feel you as a thorn pricking them, knowing you are secretly held higher than they are. So it has been with me. I am a wise-woman, and for that one sin men shut me up under various ugly names — a seed of strife, an eastern dreamer, a foreigner, a woman not easily handled. I am not so wonderfully wise. And now, to you — I am terrible. What is it you fear? What dire deed? Do I walk so proud a path — fear me not, you — that I should challenge the wrath of princes? You — what have you ever done to wrong me? You gave your daughter to the man your soul chose. Yes, him I hate out of my heart; but you, I think, have played your part well enough. I bear no grudge against your house's happiness. Go on — let her marry, and God bless your line. Only let me stay somewhere in this land. Wronged as I am, I will keep quiet, knowing my defeat.

CREON. Your words are gentle, but I am still afraid that even now some wickedness is creeping deep inside you. And so I trust you less now than before you began speaking. A woman quick to anger — yes, or a man — is easier to watch than the cold and the still. Up — find your road. Do not mock my will with words. This judgment is past recall, and none of your crafts will help you, my open enemy, to linger at my side. MEDEA [suddenly throwing herself down and clinging to CREON]. Oh, by your knees — by your newly-married daughter —
CREON. You waste your words. You will not weaken me.
MEDEA. Will you hunt me? Spurn me when I kneel to you?
CREON. My own house kneels to me — not you.
MEDEA. Home — my lost home — how I long for you now.
CREON. And I for mine, and for my child — above all things.
MEDEA. O loves of man — what a curse is on your wings.
CREON. Blessing or curse — it falls as chance has it.
MEDEA. Remember, Zeus, the cause of all this grief.
CREON. Rid me of my troubles — get up, get out.
MEDEA. What do I want with your troubles? I have my own.
CREON. Up — or by God, my soldiers here will throw —
MEDEA. Not that — not that. I am only begging, O King —
CREON. You will not go? Then I must do the harsher thing.
MEDEA. I accept my exile. That is not what I am asking.

CREON. Why so wild, then? Why clinging to my hand? MEDEA [rising]. For one day only — leave me in your land in peace, so I can find some counsel, some comfort for these two innocent ones, before the strain of exile falls on them. Others, it seems, take no thought to save the babies they have fathered. Ah — you will pity them. You also are a father; somewhere you still have a heart that feels. I am not asking for myself — it is they who break me, fallen on so terrible a day. [Exit CREON with his suite.]

CREON. I am no tyrant. Time and again my softness has spoiled the rhythm of my wisest plans. I know I am playing the fool now. So be it — you shall have this favor. But I warn you plainly: if tomorrow's sunlight finds you here within my borders — you or any child of yours — you die. Not a line of this judgment will waver or be eased. Stay on, then, if you must, until the next risen sun. No further. In one day there is scarcely time to do the deeds whose dread still haunts me.

CHORUS. O woman, woman of sorrow — where will you turn, where will you flee? What town will be yours tomorrow — what country, of all the countries that are, what door of a stranger's home? God has hunted you, Medea, out to the foam of a trackless sea. [MEDEA goes into the house.]

MEDEA. Defeat on every side — what else? But oh — this is not the end. Don't think it. I know there is one battle yet untested for the bride and groom, and good pains in store for the man who gave the bride. Do you imagine I would have groveled to this man if I had not been winning my end, shaping my plan for the work I mean to do? My lips would never have stooped to speak with him; my flesh would never have been stained by touching him. Fool — oh, triple fool. It lay so plain for him to kill my whole effort with a swift exile — and look, he gives me this one long day, in which my three enemies shall lie here dead: the father, the bride, and my own husband. Mine — not hers. I have turned over so many thoughts of murder I do not know which I like best. Shall I burn their house with fire? Or steal unseen to Jason's bedchamber — I have a blade sharpened for it — and stab the wedded pair, breast to breast? Good — except for one thing. When I am caught there and killed, my haters will laugh out loud. No — I love the old way best, the simple way of poison, where we women are as strong as any man. Ah, me. And once they are dead — what place will hold me then? What friend will rise, with land safe and trustworthy doors, to shelter this flesh from their hatred? No one — anywhere. A little longer I must wait. If some door of refuge opens, some strong tower to shield me, good — I will hunt this blood in cunning and darkness. But if my hour comes and no hope is near, then sword in hand, full-willed and certain to die, I will still live long enough to kill them. I will go like a man, their road of daring, all the way to the end. So help me she who of all the gods has been the best to me — my chosen queen and helpmate, Hecate, who dwells apart, the flame of flame in my fire's innermost heart. For all their strength, they shall not stab my soul and laugh about it afterwards. Their wedding feast shall be dark and full of grief — darkest of all the day they joined hands and hunted me away. Wake up now, Medea. Whatever plot you have, whatever cunning — strive, do not falter. To the peril-point. Now comes the strain of daring. Shall they trample you again? How? And with all of Hellas laughing at your fall, while this thief's daughter marries — and marries Jason, of all men? Your father was a true king — born of the ancient Sun. You know the way. And God has made you a woman, the most useless of things for help, but wonderful in the paths of pain.

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: CHORUS. The wave streams backward on the ever-running river. Life is changed; its laws are trampled. Man shall be the slave, the frightened, the low-liver. Man has forgotten God. And woman — yes, woman — shall be terrible in the stories told. Even the tales, I think, will run differently from before. Out of Woman comes a fear, and a glory, and the harsh, hating voices shall surround her no more. The old poets shall stop, and their old memory of frail brides and faithless wives shall be shriveled as if by fire. They did not love us, did not know us; our lips were silent, our fingers could not wake the secret of the lyre. Otherwise — otherwise, O God the Singer, I would have sung amid their fury a long tale of Man and his deeds for good and ill. But the old World knows — it is the speech of all his ages — Man's wrongs and ours; he knows, and is silent.

SOME WOMEN. From your father's home you came, O heart of fire — to the Dark Blue Rocks, to the clashing foam, to the seas of your desire. Until the Dark Blue Bar was crossed; and there, by an alien river, you stood, your lover lost, empty-armed forever. Out you go again, lowest of landless women, a wanderer of desolate ways, leaving the walls of the stranger.

OTHERS. The great Oath weakens; and Pity, struck down, has fled — fled from the shores of the Greek, away on the winds of heaven. Dark is the house far off, where an old king once called you daughter. All that was once your guiding star above stormy water — dark. And in the nearer house that swore to love you, another woman, queenlier, dearer, is throned above you. [Enter from the right JASON.]

JASON. I have often seen, in better days than these, how a dark temper makes troubles no friend can heal. It would have been easy to keep both your home and your country. All you had to do was accept the will of those who rule us, without resistance. But you, for the sheer pleasure of stormy words, are losing it all. Now your speech does not provoke me. Rail away. Of all mankind, let Jason be called the most evil — no one will stop you. But for those dark threats you have flung at the royalty of Corinth, count this exile as pure profit. When the prince's wrath was hot against you, I myself worked with all good will to soothe it, and wanted to keep you here beside me. But your mouth would not stop its vanity, day and night blaspheming our masters. So now you must flee the land. Even so, I will not hold back from helping my own. I am here, woman, to look after you, weighing your new situation carefully. I do not want you sent away with no provision — you and the children too — lacking anything I can bring you. Many lesser troubles trail at the heels of exile. And though you hate me, do not imagine my heart is capable of any anger toward you. [She catches sight of her own hand which she has thrown out to denounce him.]

MEDEA. Evil — most evil. Since you grant me this comfort, the worst weapon left to me now is to strike a coward. You — coming here — you, my enemy. [Turning to the CHORUS.] Tell me, what do you call this — facing and smiling at the comrade whose kiss betrayed her? Scorn? Insult? Courage? None of these. It is the vilest of all man's inward sicknesses — that he knows neither shame nor pity. And yet I am glad he came. It will give me comfort, just once, to clear my heart on you, and you shall wince to hear it. Let me begin with the first thing that happened between you and me. I saved you. I saved you — let your own Greeks, every one who sailed on the Argo, bear witness. I saved you when you were sent alone to yoke the bulls of fiery breath, to sow that Acre of the Lords of Death. And my own ancient Serpent, who guarded the Golden Fleece, those eyes that never slept, those shining coils — him also I struck dead for your sake, and lifted up the light that gave you life. By myself, with no one's counsel, I stole away from my father and my home, and fled with you to where dark Iolcus lies under Pelion — single-hearted more than wise. I murdered Pelias, in agony, by his own daughters' hands, for your sake; I swept their house like War. And after taking all of that — O evil yet again — you cast me off and have taken yourself another bride. And with children at your side. One could forgive a childless man. But no — I have borne you children. Is sworn faith such a low and feeble thing? I do not understand it. Are the old gods dead? Are the old laws forgotten and new ones made? It cannot be only my passion that calls you forsworn — your own heart must say it too. Poor right hand of mine, that he clasped so often, and these knees he clung to so cravingly — we are unclean, you and I; we have caught the stain of bad men's flesh, and dreamed our dreams in vain. You come to befriend me? Then give me your counsel. Not because I dream of any good from you — but if I question you, you will only reveal the viler man. Tell me — where shall I go now? Back to my father? I betrayed him, and his whole country, when we two fled. To those poor daughters of Pelias? It would be lovely for them to take me in — me who spilled their father's blood. So my whole life stands. There were people at home who loved me well; to them I have become a curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, the ones I should most have spared, I turned into enemies for your sake. So this is the crown you have set on me, the woman blessed beyond every Greek girl, now that I have won what they all longed for — you, the world-famous lover, the brave one — who looks at me today and sees me banished, thrown away with these two babies, all alone. Oh, the merry mockery when the lamps are lit: "Where do the bridegroom's babies go to beg their bread in exile, with the woman who gave everything to save him?" O great God — gold can be tested, marked clearly to tell base from fine — but on a man's living face there is no sign to show the lie inside, until it is too late.
LEADER. Terrible and beyond healing is the hatred when hearts that loved each other turn into enemies.

JASON. In speech, at least, I think I had better not be a poor pilot. Like an old captain who furls his sail to the last edge when too fierce a danger blows, I will run before the wind and swell of your loud storms — woman — and tell my story this way. Since you build so high your acts of service to me in my danger — I know of only one savior, of all gods or mortals, of the whole quest and crew: the Cyprian. You have brain and wit, but underneath — well, the whole tale would be graceless to tell: how sheer love, a fire of poison-shafts, drove you with desire to save me. Enough. I will not score that count too closely. It was good help, and I thank you for it, however it came about. But in saving me, you got far more than you gave. A good Greek country has been your lasting home, not barbarian land. You have seen our ordered life, our justice, the long steady grasp of law that does not change at the strong man's pleasure. And all of Hellas, far and near, has come to know your wisdom; in every ear your fame is. If your days had passed unseen on that last edge of the world, where would the story of great Medea be? You and I — what would treasures piled high in rich kings' rooms be worth to us, what worth a voice of gold sweeter than ever rang from old Orpheus, unless our deeds had glory? I speak this way only because, on the matter of the Quest I accomplished, you yourself threw the challenge down. Now for your bitter complaint about my alliance with a king. Here you will see I was both wise and clear of any passion, and a most powerful friend to you and to my children. No — be still. When I first stood here in Corinth, weighed down with one desperate misfortune after another, what stroke of luck could I have dreamed of like this — to marry a king's daughter, I, an exile and a beggar? Not (as your wild jealousy imagines) out of any loathing for your bed; not out of any extra love for this new bride; not because I wanted to build up my house with more children. What you have borne is enough; I make no fuss about it. But, first and greatest, I wanted us all to live in a fair house and lack for nothing — knowing well that poor men have no friends, only avoidance and silence on every side. Next, I wanted to raise our sons in a manner worthy of my line, and by giving them brothers to bring my two houses together, joining them all into one and making us all from now on prince-like and happy. What more do you need of children? And for me, it suits my fortune to bind in strength the children that are with the children to come. Have I planned badly? Even you would not say so, if you could quiet your jealous flesh for one hour. But it is always so. Who looks for more from women? When the flow of love runs smooth, the whole world is fair. But let any ill chance break the thirst, and men's dearest aims, their noblest, are trampled in swift hate. By God, if only we mortals could raise our children from some other seed, and there were no blind women blocking our way. Then there would be no curse on humankind.

LEADER. Lord Jason, you have woven your speech very subtly. But still — though I speak against your will — what you are doing is not right. It is wrong: you betray the woman who loved you and was true.

MEDEA. I have my thoughts, plenty of them, and many have made me odd to others. To me it seems that when a crafty tongue is given to evil men, it is more likely to wreck them than to help. Their own brain tempts them with lies to dare and dare again, until — no man has subtlety enough. As you — do not look so fair to me, do not be so deft of speech. One word will make you fall. If you had not been false, your part was to tell me everything, ask me to support your marriage path, since I loved you — not to fool me with a lie.
JASON. An easy task that would have been — and you a loving aid, who cannot, even now, still that loud heart of yours surging like the tide.
MEDEA. That was not what moved you. Your old barbarian bride, the dog from the east who loved you so, was growing grey-haired — she no longer flattered your pride.

JASON. Understand, just once. The girl is nothing to me in this web of sovereignty I am building. I am only trying to save you, even still. And to give brothers to our sons — to father young kings, so that we may all prosper again.
MEDEA. God shield me from prosperous days that bring pain, and wealth that opens wounds in my heart.
JASON. Will you change that prayer and choose a wiser part? Pray not to mistake good sense for pain, nor to call yourself unhappy when you are too lucky.
MEDEA. Yes, mock me — you have somewhere to lay your head, and I go naked to my exile.
JASON. Walk your own road. You have made it what it is.
MEDEA. How — by seducing and abandoning you?
JASON. By those vile curses you let loose on the royal hall —
MEDEA. And on your house also — wherever the chance falls — I am a living curse.

JASON. Peace — enough of these futile quarrels. I will have no more of them. If you will take, from all I have, anything to help these babies and your own helplessness in exile, name it. I stand here ready to help you with an unsparing hand, and to send my signet to old friends abroad who will treat you well. Refuse, and you do a useless thing. But cast your rage aside and you stand to gain much — and lose little — by reining in your anger.
MEDEA. I will not seek out your friends. I will not take what you give. Do not give it. Fruit from an unholy stem brings no blessing. [He goes slowly away.]

JASON. Now God in heaven be witness — my whole heart is willing to do its part for you and for your children. But nothing good can please you. In sheer savageness of mood you drive every friend away. So I warn you — your pains will only be the greater for it.

MEDEA. Go — you are restless for the new delight you are courting, having stayed so long out of sight of her sweet chamber. Go, fulfill your pride, O bridegroom. For perhaps such a bride is waiting for you — and God hears me in this — that your own heart will sicken before it kisses her.

CHORUS. Alas — the Love that falls like a flood, strong-winged and fleeting — why do you praise him? What good does he bring to man, what glory? But there is a Love that moves in gentleness, heart-filling, sweetest of all powers that bless. Do not loose on me, O Holder of man's heart, your golden quiver; do not steep in the poison of desire the dart that never heals. The pent-up hatred of the carping word, the strife with no end, where once was tenderness; the mad heart's breath panting after a stranger — O Cyprian, do not cast me into these. Sift, sharp-eyed, between love's good gift and its evil. Make Innocence my friend — God's fairest star — and do not lessen the rare sweet beat of bosoms without war, who love and do not hate. [While MEDEA is waiting downcast, seated upon her doorstep, a traveler with followers passes from the left. As he catches sight of MEDEA, he stops.]

OTHERS. Home of my heart, land of my own — do not, for pity's sake, cast me out on my ways, helpless, alone, where the feet fail in the mire and the stones, a woman without a city. Not that — better the end. Let the green grave cover me sooner, if there must be a break in the days I know, and the skies be changed and the earth below them. The weariest road a man can walk is the road out of his father's home. Look — we have seen it. This is not a song heard somewhere, learned from another. Whom do you have, in your most terrible wrong, for comfort? Never a strong city to hide you, never a brother. Ah — but the man — cursed be he, cursed past recovery, who breaks open, seal by seal, a friend's clean heart, and then turns his heel away, deaf to love. He shall find in me no friend and no lover.

AEGEUS. Joy to you, Medea. It is the homeliest word old friends can greet each other with, and the best. MEDEA [looking up, surprised]. And joy to you, Aegeus, gentle king of Athens. Where are you traveling from?
AEGEUS. From Delphi just now — the old cavern with its stairs.
MEDEA. Where Earth's heart speaks in song? What were you doing there?
AEGEUS. Praying heaven for children — the same old search.
MEDEA. Children? My God — you are still childless?
AEGEUS. So God has willed. Childless and desolate.
MEDEA. What word did Phoebus speak, to change your fate?
AEGEUS. Riddles — too hard for a mortal man to read.
MEDEA. May I hear them?
AEGEUS. Of course — they need a sharper wit than mine.
MEDEA. What did he say?
AEGEUS. Not to spill life's wine, not to seek for more —
MEDEA. Until?
AEGEUS. Until I tread the hearth-stone of my forefathers.
MEDEA. And what brings you here, by Creon's shore?
AEGEUS. Do you know one Pittheus, the high lord of Trozen?
MEDEA. Yes — Pelops' son, a man most pure of sin.
AEGEUS. I want to ask him about Apollo's meaning.
MEDEA. He is much practiced in the gods' ways, and very skilled.
AEGEUS. Long years ago, he was my battle-friend — the truest a man ever had.
MEDEA. Well, may God grant you good fortune and all you desire.
AEGEUS. But you — you look wasted, the fire dead in your eyes.
MEDEA. Aegeus — my husband is the falsest man in the world.
AEGEUS. What are you saying? Tell me clearly what has darkened your face.
MEDEA. He is false to me — and I never harmed him.
AEGEUS. What has he done? Tell me everything.
MEDEA. He has taken a wife — set her over me, to rule his house.
AEGEUS. Jason — has not dared to do a thing so shameful?
MEDEA. He has. And those he loved before have no place now.
AEGEUS. Some passion has swept him? Or is it you he is turning from?
MEDEA. Passion — passion to betray those dearest to him.
AEGEUS. Shame on him for falling so far from honor.
MEDEA. Passion to be near a throne — to be a king's heir.
AEGEUS. Who is giving him the bride? Tell me.
MEDEA. Creon — chief over all Corinth.
AEGEUS. Woman, you have indeed great cause for grief.
MEDEA. It is ruin. And they have cast me out as well.
AEGEUS. Who? This is a new wrong — a terrible one.
MEDEA. Creon the king — banished from every land and shore —
AEGEUS. And Jason allows it? This is too much.

MEDEA. He bears such things bravely. But Aegeus — by your beard, by your knees, I beg you, I make myself your suppliant: pity me. Pity a woman so miserable. Do not, do not let me stand here and be cast out friendless to despair. Give me a home in Athens — by the fire of your own hearth. So may your desire for children be fulfilled by God, and may you die a happy man. You do not yet know it — but already the prize is won. I, I will make a childless man of you no more. The seed shall be sown — I swear it. Such magic herbs I know.

AEGEUS. Woman, my heart truly goes out to give you this help — first for religion's sake, then for your promised hope, to heal my ache of childlessness. That is what has made my whole life a shadow and starved my soul. But this is how it stands with me. Once you make your way to Attic earth, I, by law, will keep you and befriend you. But in this country, where Creon rules, I cannot raise my hand to shelter you. Come of your own initiative to my house, and there you will stay forever, inviolate, never to be seized again. But come from Corinth on your own. I want to be seen as just, even by foreign eyes.
MEDEA. That is well. Give me an oath I can trust, and you have granted everything a man could ask.
AEGEUS. Do you not trust me? What troubles you?

MEDEA. I trust you. But so many, far and near, hate me — King Pelias' whole house, and here, Creon. Once you are bound by oaths and sanctities, you cannot give me up to people like these to be dragged out of Athens. But a spoken word, no more, to bind you — one no god has heard — well, embassies could come and go: they are all friends to you. Ah, I know you will not listen to me. So weak am I, and they so full of gold and majesty.

AEGEUS. This is a long-sighted oath you ask. Still, if you will have it, I am perfectly willing to serve you. My own hand is the stronger if I have this excuse to show your persecutors — and the bond is more sure for you. By what god shall I swear?
MEDEA. Swear by the Earth you walk on, by the Sun, the father of my fathers, and by all the gods together —
AEGEUS. To do — or not to do — what? Make it plain.
MEDEA. Never to cast me out yourself, nor let any other, on whatever pretext, take me from your land while you live and are free.
AEGEUS. Never. Hear me, Earth, and the great star of daylight, and all the other gods.
MEDEA. It is well. And if you should fail your vow —
AEGEUS. May God's judgment on the godless break my brow. [AEGEUS and his train depart.]
MEDEA. Go — go your way rejoicing. Now everything is bright and clear before me. Go — and before night I will follow, when the deed I plan is done and the end I thirst for is won.

CHORUS. Farewell. May Maia's guiding Son lead you back to your hearth and fire, Aegeus; and may the long desire that wastes you be at last fulfilled. Our eyes have seen you as you are — a gentle and a righteous heart.

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: MEDEA. God — and God's Justice — and you blinding Skies. At last my victory is dawning. My eyes see it now, and my foot stands on the mountain's brow. My enemies — my enemies — now atonement is coming. Here at my worst hour a friend has been found, a very port of safety to save my shipwreck. Here I will make fast my anchor and escape them at the last, in the walled hill of Athens. But before the end, my friend, it is right that I show you my whole plan — take it, this is no tale to make people laugh. I will send some servant straight to Jason, to ask him to come to me. When he is here, I will feed his ear with soft reasons — how his will is now my will, how everything is well concerning this royal marriage-bed for which I have been betrayed: all wise and rare and profitable. And then I will make one request — that my two children should not be exiled but stay behind. Not that I would leave a child of mine on these angry shores for those who hate me to laugh at; no — it is so that I can kill the king's daughter by cunning. They shall be sent with gifts, gifts to the bride to spare their exile: fine robes and a golden necklace. Once she takes that raiment and wraps it around her, a foul death she shall die — that girl, and everyone who touches her in her agony. Such is the poison they shall drink, my robe and wreath. But enough of that. I grind my teeth thinking of the path my feet must walk after that. I shall lay those children dead — my own children, whom no hand shall steal from me. Then, leaving Jason childless, the day above him as black as night, I shall go my road into exile — fleeing, fleeing from the blood of my best beloved — having done every horrible thing, so long as one thing does not reach me: the laughter of those who hate us. Let it come. What is life worth to me now? I have no home, no country anymore, no shield against any wrong. That was my evil hour, when I stole out down the long halls of my father, my will chained by a Greek man's voice — who still, oh, still, if God lives, shall be paid back in full. For Jason shall never see another child of mine alive after this; never father a child on his new bride, who today, desolate as she made me desolate, shall die screaming amid my poisons. Have I a name among your people? Am I a feeble thing, weak of hand, an eastern dreamer? No — I am branded with the burn of strange suns. My hate, by God above, is a dangerous thing, and my love passing sweet. These are what make a life glorious.
LEADER. Since you have bared this savage purpose to us, I, who love you and who must defend the laws of men, beg you — do not dream of this deed.
MEDEA. There is no other way. I forgive you your smallness — you have not been wronged as I have.
LEADER. You cannot kill the fruit of your own body.
MEDEA. Yes — if it pains the man I hate the more.
LEADER. And makes you the most miserable of all? [She claps her hands; the NURSE comes out from the house. The NURSE departs.]

MEDEA. Let it come. All words of good or ill are wasted now. Woman, go — bring Lord Jason here. There is no one like you to do me these high services. But say not a word about my purpose, as you are faithful — and bold to try every help — and a woman, just as I am.

CHORUS. The sons of Erechtheus, the ancient ones, whom high gods planted long ago in an old land upheld by heaven, a proud land untrodden by war: they are hungered, and look — their hunger is fed with wisdom as with meat. In their skies a fire shines; in the fall of their feet there is joy. And there, with many gifts, from the North, from the hills, from the morning, the Muses gathered their powers, so that a child of the Nine should be born. And Harmony, sown like flowers, grew golden in the fields of grain. And Cephisus, the fair-flowing river — the Cyprian dipped her hand and drew its dew, and the shiver of her touch is like joy in the land. For her breathing is written in fragrance, and in music her path as she goes, and the cloud of her hair is lit with stars of the wind-woven rose. So she goes forever and ever, and out of her bosom is blown, like dew on the winds of the river, a hunger of unknown passions. Strong Loves of every godlike endeavor — whom Wisdom shall enthrone beside her on her throne.

SOME WOMEN. But Cephisus the fair-flowing — will he bear you on his shore? Shall the land that helps all comers help you — you who are foul among your kind, with the tears of blinded children on you? Do you see the red gash growing? Do you see what you carry? On every side, every way — look, we kneel to you and pray: by your knees, by your soul, O wild woman — one at least you cannot kill — not your child.

OTHERS. Do you have ice that you would bind it to your breast, and go dead to your children, to your own spirit's pain? When the hand knows what it dares, when your eyes look into theirs — shall you keep, unblinded by tears, your dividing of the slain? These are not deeds for you. These are things that cannot be. Your children — however fierce your courage, when they cling about your knees, you will fail. [Enter JASON.]

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: JASON. I have come at your call. However full of hate you may be, I will not lessen my kindness toward you nor refuse to listen. Tell me what new thing you wanted, that you sent for me. [The CHILDREN come from the house, followed by their ATTENDANT. As the CHILDREN go to JASON, MEDEA suddenly bursts into tears. The CHILDREN quickly return to her; she recovers herself, smiling through her tears. She wipes the child's face.]

MEDEA. Jason, I beg you — for the words I just spoke, forgive me. My bad moods — at least you will try to bear with them. There have been many old deeds of love between you and me. I have reasoned with myself in private and scolded myself: "Why must I be mad, my heart, raging against a man whose word is wisdom — making myself a thing detested by those who rule the land, and by my own husband, who is doing only what, once done, will help us all? He marries a queen and gives my sons young kings as brothers. Yet I rage on alone and cannot let my rage go. What is wrong with me, when God sends so simple a refuge? Have I not my children? Don't I know that we are only exiles, who must go begging and friendless otherwise?" Thought after thought pressed me, until I knew myself fully laden with bitterness of heart and blinded eyes. So now — I thank you, and I think you wise to have caught this anchor for our help. I was the fool — I should have been your friend, your tool; should have gone wooing with you, stood beside your bed in service, and dutifully welcomed your bride. But we are what we are. I will not say merely evil — but women. You should not, today, turn strange and become some childish, evil thing in answer to my childish passion. Look — I yield. I confess I had bad thoughts before, but now I have turned around and found my wiser mind. [She claps her hands.] Children — run, quickly. Come out here into the sunshine, and greet your father. Welcome him along with us. Throw away, throw away — utterly, as your mother does — your anger against one so dear. Our peace is made, the old bad war shall stop forever. Go, and take his hand. Ah me — I am full of hidden horrors. Will it be a long time still, my children, that you live to put those dear, dear arms around me? Forgive me — I am so ready with my tears today, so full of dread. I tried to smooth away the long quarrel with your father, and now I have flooded this little forehead with tears.
LEADER. A pale tear is creeping into my eyes too. Let the evil rest, O God — let it rest here.

JASON. Woman, I praise you for this, and say no ill of how you behaved before. It is nature's way — a woman must work herself up to anger when her husband's marriage business takes some strange new path across her. But your heart has now found the happier road. You have seen, before the very end, what choice must be the stronger — and to do that shows a wise-minded woman. As for you, children — your father has not forgotten what you need. With God's help I have worked out a strong deliverance for your weakness. I think that you, with your brothers, will one day be the mightiest voices in this land. Grow tall and strong. Your father's hand guides everything else, and whatever divine power has always helped him. May it be mine to see you yet in your manhood, stern of brow, strong-armed, set above those who hate me. — But — woman, your face is turned away. Your cheek is washed with the pallor of strange tears. Do you not gladly and willingly accept my blessings?
MEDEA. It is nothing — I was thinking of these little ones.
JASON. Take heart, then. I will guard them from all harm.
MEDEA. I do take heart. I will never mistrust your word. Alas, a woman's bosom carries only a woman's courage — a thing born for tears.
JASON. What is wrong? You are weeping too bitterly there.

MEDEA. I was their mother. When I heard your prayer of long life for them, a horror swept over me, wondering how these things shall be. But for the matter I needed to speak to you about — part I have said, and now I will finish. Since it is the king's command to cast me out of Corinth — yes, and best, far best for me, I know it, not to stay here longer to trouble you and those who rule the realm, who consider me a foe to all their house — look, I spread my sails and meekly go to exile. But our children — could this land still be their home awhile? Could your own hand guide their boyhood? Go to the king and beg his pity, that he may let your children stay.
JASON. He is hard to move. But surely it would be well done.
MEDEA. Bid her — for your sake, ask the daughter for this favor.
JASON. Well thought. Her I can shape to my mind. [A handmaid goes into the house. The handmaid returns bearing the Gifts.]

MEDEA. Yes — she is a woman, like the rest of us. And I will help you in your effort. I will send her gifts — the fairest gifts in the hands of men, things from the days of old, fine robes and a golden necklace, by the boys' hands. Quick — some handmaiden — go fetch the raiment. Ah, her cup will be filled indeed. What more should a woman desire — married to you, the bravest of the brave, dressed in robes that the father of all my house, the Sun himself, gave, steeped in fire, to his own fiery descendants? Come, children — lift these caskets carefully. Carry them as your gift to her, who is bride and princess and rightly blessed. I think she will not hold them lightly.

JASON. Foolish woman, why empty your hand of treasure like this? Does King Creon's castle lack for raiment, or for gold? Keep these — make no gift. If she values Jason at all, I swear, things like these will not weigh more with her than I do. [She goes quickly into the house. JASON and the CHILDREN with their ATTENDANT depart.]

MEDEA. Ah, do not scold me. It is written: gifts persuade the gods in heaven, and gold is stronger than countless words to bend men's ways. Fortune is hers. God makes her days great — young, and a crowned queen. And exile for those two babies. I would rather it were not gold spent than that — I would rather spend life's blood. My children, go into those rich halls, and bowing low, beg your father's bride — to whom I now bow — that of her mercy you not be cast out into exile. And give her the caskets — above all, mark this — to no one but her, into her own hands to keep. Quick — go. And let your mother soon hear the good news she longs for. Go.

CHORUS. Now I have no hope left for the children's lives — no hope. They are gone forth to their death. The bride takes the poison they bring. She takes the gold band and opens it; and she lifts the crown — the crown — about her brow, where the light brown curls are clustering. No hope now. O sweet and clouded gleam of the golden garments. The robe has clasped her breast, the crown her head. Now, now, she dresses for a wedding — like a bride out of an old story going pale to a kiss with the dead. The ring has closed; her share of death is in it. She does not flee — she perishes unaware.

SOME WOMEN. O bridegroom, bridegroom of the kiss so cold — are you wedded with princes? Are you girt with gold — and yet, all unknowing, suing for your child's undoing, and for an unspeakable doom on the woman you love? How fallen you are from your old place. [Enter the ATTENDANT with the two CHILDREN. MEDEA comes out from the house.]

OTHERS. O Mother, Mother — what is yours to reap when the harvest comes, between waking and sleeping? For an unslaked heart, for a broken vow — look, babies who call you from a bloody pit, and your love returns no more. Go forth and weep.

ATTENDANT. Mistress — these children are spared their banishment. The royal bride has graciously accepted your gifts with her own hand, and all is now peace for the children. Why do you stand there confounded, when good fortune is at hand?
MEDEA. Oh God.
ATTENDANT. That does not match the news I bring.
MEDEA. O God, have mercy.
ATTENDANT. Is some word of anger hidden here that I did not know about? Has my hope of bringing you joy fooled me?
MEDEA. You give what you give. I do not blame you.
ATTENDANT. Your face is overcast — your eyes are filling.
MEDEA. Out of bitter need, old man. The gods have willed it, and my own evil mind, that this should come.
ATTENDANT. Take heart — your sons will bring you home one day.
MEDEA. Home? I have others to send home. Woe is me.

ATTENDANT. Be patient. Many a mother before you has been parted from her children. We poor things called men must endure what fortune brings. [The ATTENDANT goes into the house. A handmaid brings the CHILDREN out again. MEDEA has kept them hitherto at arm's length, but at the touch of their hands her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms. She follows the CHILDREN into the house.]

MEDEA. I will endure. — Go inside, and lay everything ready that my sons will need today. O children, children of mine — you have found a land and a home, where you will stay forever, leaving me uncrowned and desolate — motherless children. And I go my way to other lands, an exile, before you bring your fruits home, before I see you prospering, before I know your brides or deck the bridal bed with flowers, or hold your torches overhead. Oh, cursed be my own hard heart. It was all in vain, then, that I raised you up so tall and fair — in vain I carried you and was torn with those long, merciless pains when you were born. Ah, the wonderful hopes my poor heart had for you — how you would tend me in my old age, and lay the shroud about me with your own dear hands, when I lay cold, blessed in every land that knew us. And that gentle thought is dead. You go, and I live on, to eat the bread of long years, my own pain unending. Never again will those dear eyes see their mother, far away, thrown into other shapes of life. My babies — my own — why do you look at me like that? What is it you see? And why laugh with that last laughter? Woe is me, what shall I do? Women — my strength is gone, gone like a dream, since I looked at those shining faces. I cannot do it. Good-bye to all the thoughts that burned so hot before. I will take them and hide them far, far from men's eyes. Why should I wage so blind a war — to sting their father's heart through these babies' wounds and win myself a pain twice as deep? Never, never. From now on I forget all I worked for. And yet — what is happening to me? Will I be a thing to be mocked, and leave my enemies to sting on, unsmitten? It must be. O coward heart, ever to harbor such soft words. Get out of my sight, you two. [The CHILDREN go in.] And those whose eyes will count it sin to share my sacrifice — let it be on their heads. My hand will not swerve now. Ah, ah — Wrath within me — do not — do not. Down, down, you tortured thing, and spare my children. They will live with us, far off, and give you peace. Too late, too late. By all Hell's living agonies of hate, they shall not take my little ones alive to make a mockery. However I struggle, the thing is doomed; it cannot escape now from being done. Yes — the crown is on her brow, the robe is wrapped about her, and in that robe the high Queen is dying. I know it all. Yet — since I must go on so long a journey, and these two on a longer and darker one — I would speak with them once before I go. Come, children — stand a little away from me. There. Reach out your hand — your right hand — so — to mother. Good-bye. Oh, darling hand. Oh, darling mouth, darling eye, and royal bearing, and bright brave clear faces — may you be blessed, but not here. Whatever was yours here, your father stole. Ah, God — the glow of cheek on cheek, the tender touch — and oh, the sweet scent of childhood. Go. Go. Am I blind? My eyes can see nothing when I look to find their places. I am broken by the wings of evil. Yes, I know what bad things I am going to. But louder than all thought, Anger cries — Anger, which makes man's worst misery. [MEDEA comes out alone from the house.]

CHORUS. My thoughts have roamed in a cloudy country, and heard a fiercer music falling than a woman's heart should stir to. And yet some majestic Muse, unknown, has taken hold of woman's hand, seeking for Wisdom — not in everyone: a feeble seed, a scattered band — but you may yet find it in lonely places, not dead among us, our faces not always turned away from the Muses' call. And so my thought would speak: she who has never borne a child, and never known one, is closer to happiness. She walks unlit and alone, with little understanding of what a child's touch means in joy or in sorrow, and she carries none of the toils. But those in whose fair garden that gentle plant has flowered — they go through their days deep-written all over with care: rearing the children, securing their hold, winning them wealth — and then so much darkness, if at last the seed bears fruit in good men or in evil. And there is one thing at the end of all things that all men dread. The wealth is won, the limbs are grown to manhood, the heart honest as well — and look, where Fortune smiled, some change, and what has fallen? Listen — it is death slowly winging to the dark, and in his arms what was your child. So what gain does this bring to man, whose cup was already full, that God should send this one thing more — of hunger and of dread, a door set wide to every wind of pain? [Enter MESSENGER.]

MEDEA. Friends, this long hour I have been waiting on Fortune's eyes, straining my senses in a hot surmise about what is happening on that hill. Ah — even now there comes — one of Jason's men, I think. His wildly disturbed breath tells me the news of some strange disaster.

chapters.title: Exodos
paragraphs: MESSENGER. O dire and ghastly deed. Get away, Medea. Fly. Don't leave behind one chariot's wing, one keel that sweeps the seas —
MEDEA. What has happened to send you running like this?
MESSENGER. The maiden princess lies dead — and her father, the king — both murdered by your poison-fire.
MEDEA. Most happy news. From this day on, your name shall stand among my friends and well-wishers.
MESSENGER. What are you saying? Woman — is your mind clear, not raving? You are caught in a most bloody crime against the king's own person — and you laugh at the news, you have no fear?

MEDEA. I have words too that could answer yours well enough. But take your ease, good friend, and tell me — how did they die? Was it a very foul death, please? That would be a comfort to my soul. [Exit MESSENGER.]

MESSENGER. When your two children, hand in hand, came in with their father and walked through into the new bridal rooms, oh, we were glad — we slaves who always loved you well, who grieved in your grief. And straight away the word went from ear to ear that you and your false lord had poured a peace-offering over your old quarrel. We gave them a glad welcome; one of us kissed the small hand, another the shining hair. I, for sheer joy, followed where the women's rooms are. There our mistress — she whom we now call by that name — sat waiting for Jason, with a glad and eager brow, not thinking she would see your two little ones. Then she saw them, and slowly veiled her eyes, and turned her face away — sick to think your children were coming near her. Then your husband quickly stepped forward to soothe the young woman's fitful anger. "You will not meet love's coming with unkindness? Restrain your suddenness, turn your face back to us — hold as friends those dear to me. Accept these robes they bring as gifts, and beg your father to lift the sentence of exile from them, for my sake." The moment she saw the raiment, she could hold back her joy no longer, and gave him everything he asked. And almost before the father and the two children were out of the room, she pulled out the embroidered garments and sat down to dress herself: bound the golden crown through her long curls, and arranged the separate clusters in a fair mirror, smiling at her own dead self facing her there. Then she pushed her chair aside and walked through those wide chambers alone, her white foot poising delicately — she was so happy with the gifts. Many a time she paused, straight-limbed, and turned her head to watch the long fold sweeping to her heel. And then something strange came over her. Her cheek seemed to go pale; with crooked, weak steps and arms groping, she walked back, and barely made her seat — she nearly fell to the ground. Among the handmaids was an old grey woman who thought, I think, that Pan had taken hold of her, or some spirit, and raised a keen, piercing cry of warning. But then white foam was seen crawling through her lips, her eyeballs rolled back, and her face went dead pale, drained of life. While the old woman was still calling, the cry turned strangely to its opposite, dying away in sobs. Then one of us flew off swiftly to find her father's rooms, another to the new bridegroom, to tell the tale. The whole place was loud with hurrying feet. As long as a swift walker on a measured course would take to pace a furlong, she lay there speechless, with closed lids. Then she opened her eyes wide, and as she struggled to rise, gave a wild shriek — for two different waves of stabbing death were rolling over her. The golden necklace that gripped her brow was melting in a dire, wondrous river of devouring fire. And those fine robes — the gift your children gave her — God's mercy — everywhere lapped and washed her delicate flesh. Up she sprang and fled, a fiery pillar, shaking head and hair this way and that, trying to throw the crown somewhere clear. But the burning gold held the diadem fast, like a thing nailed down; and through her hair, the more she shook it loose, the fiercer came the fire, until she fell to earth — a thing scarcely nameable, except to her father — and struggled no more. That cheek of royal beauty — where was it? Or the place where her eyes had been? Only from her crown and temples came faint blood shot through with fire. The very flesh stood out from the bones like the gum that starts from a wounded pine, where those subtle gnawing poisons bit in the dark — a ghastly sight. We did not dare touch the dead. We had seen too much. But that poor father, knowing nothing, had hurried to his daughter's room, and there the dead lay at his feet. He knelt, and groaning low, folded her in his arms and kissed her: "Unhappy child — what unnatural thing has so hideously undone you? What divine wrath would make this old grey grave childless of you? Would God lay me there to die with you, my daughter." So he cried. But after, when he stopped weeping and tried to lift his old bent frame, he was held in the folds of those fine robes — as ivy holds, strangling, among laurel boughs. Then a ghastly struggle began. Again and again he tried to rise on his knee — but that dead breast clung to his. And at last, like a man possessed, he wrenched himself half free; and the living flesh tore away, and he laid himself down to fight death no more, but to die. The deep had risen above his soul. And there they sleep at last, the old proud father and the bride, side by side — just as his tears had asked. As for you — no more words. You yourself will know how best to balk vengeance. Long ago I looked at man's days and found a grey shadow. And this much I will say: those of all men counted wise — the strong wits, the devisers of great policies — pay the bitterest price. Since life began, has there ever been one happy man in God's eye? Fair days roll on, and bring more or fewer gifts of fortune, but to no man happiness.
SOME WOMEN. Wrath upon wrath, I think, will fall today from God on Jason — he has earned it all.

OTHER WOMEN. O wretched maiden — my whole heart is torn for you, that you have so suddenly gone from your king's chambers and the light above into darkness, all for the sake of Jason's love. [She goes into the house.]

MEDEA. Women, my mind is clear. I go to kill my children with all speed, and then away from here — not to wait until they stand under another, angrier hand to die. Yes — however I shield them, die they must. And since they must, I — their mother — will kill them. No other hand. Up — put your armor on, my heart. Why do we hesitate any longer to win the crown of dire, inevitable sin? Take up your sword, my poor right hand, your sword. Then on, to the thin-drawn line where life turns into agony. Let there be no softness now. Keep yourself from that thought — "Born of your flesh — your own beloved." For one short day, forget your children — you can weep afterwards. Even though you kill them, they were sweet. I am sore unfortunate.

SOME WOMEN. O Earth, our mother — and you, All-seer, the arrowy crown of Sunlight — look down on man now, oh, look down. Look upon one accursed, before in blood she twines red hands — blood that is your own. O Sun, save her first. She is still your daughter, of your own golden line — save her. Or shall man spill the divine life? Give peace, O Fire that does not die — send your spell to stop her yet, to lift her far, far away — a spirit changed by torture, a voice out of Hell wrought of old wrongs and war. [A cry is heard within.]

OTHERS. Alas — the mother's pain wasted. Alas the dear life born for nothing. Woman — what are you doing here, you who came from beyond the Gate where the dim Symplegades clash in the dark blue seas, the shores where death waits? Why have you taken on yourself, to make us desolate, this anger of misery and this guilt of hate? Fierce are the strikes back of blood once shed where love has been: God's wrath upon the killers, an anguished earth, and the wonder of the dead haunting on like music.
A WOMAN. Listen — did you hear? Did you hear the children's cry?
ANOTHER. O wretched woman — accursed.
A CHILD WITHIN. What shall I do? What is it? Keep me away from mother.
THE OTHER CHILD. I don't know — brother. I think she means to kill us.
A WOMAN. Let me go — I will — Help. Help. Save them at the last.
A CHILD. Yes, in God's name — help, quickly, before we die. [Many of the Women are now beating at the barred door to get in. Others stand apart.]
THE OTHER CHILD. She has almost caught me now. She has a sword.
WOMEN AT THE DOOR. You stone — you thing of iron. Will you really spill with your own hand that life — the vintage stored from your own agony? [Enter hurriedly JASON and Attendants.]

THE OTHER WOMEN. A Mother killed her babies once, in days of old — one, only one, from dawn to evening — Ino, god-maddened, whom the Queen of Heaven sent in a frenzy flying to the dark. She threw herself for sorrow into the wide salt sea, out of those rooms of unforgiven murder, wild-footed from a white crag of the shore — and clasping her two children still, she died. O Love of Woman, charged with such heavy sorrow — what have you wrought upon us? What more is left to fear?

JASON. You women clustering at this doorway — speak. Is the doer of this ghastly thing still here, or fled? What hope has she of flight? Will the deep open to shield her? Will the height send her wings to hide her in the vault of the sky, after working red murder on her lords, so she gets away unpunished? Let her go. My care is to save my children — not to find her. Let those she wronged pay her back as they may. I do not care. It is my sons I must somehow save, before the dead king's kinsmen can win from them payment for their mother's sin.
LEADER. Unhappy man — you do not know what dark place you have come to. Otherwise, Jason, no such words could fall from your lips.
JASON. What is it? Does the woman want to kill me too?
LEADER. Your sons are dead — slain by their mother's hand.
JASON. What? Not the children — I scarcely understand. O God — you have broken me.
LEADER. Think of those two as things once fair, that will never bloom again.
JASON. Where did she murder them? In that old room?

LEADER. Open the door, and you will see your children's doom. [While the Attendants are still battering at the door, MEDEA appears on the roof, standing on a chariot of winged Dragons in which lie the children's bodies.]
JASON. You — slaves — unbar that door. Faster. Wrench the door from its hinges. Show me my two-edged curse — the dead children — the woman. Oh, this sword on her head —

MEDEA. What are you doing at my gates? Why do you batter with brazen bars, looking for the dead and for me, who killed them? Peace. And you — if you need anything of mine, speak — though your touch shall never harm me again. Out of his firmament my fathers' father, the high Sun, has sent this thing — to save me from my enemies' rage.

JASON. You living hate. Wife abhorred in every age. Blood-red mother, who killed my sons and made me as good as dead — and still you can take the sunlight on your eyes, smell the green earth, reeking from your hellish deed. I curse you. Now, oh, now my eyes can see, that were blinded then — when out of the savagery of eastern chambers, out of a cruel land, I gathered you up to bring to Greece and home — you, the curse made flesh — a woman who betrayed her home, her father, her — oh, God has laid your sins on me. I knew, I knew, there lay a brother murdered on your hearth that day when your first footstep fell on Argo's hull. Argo — my own — my swift and beautiful — that was her first beginning. Then I made her my wife in my house. She gave birth to children — and now, for the sake of love, of the bedchamber and a man's arms, she has murdered them. A thing not one of all the maids of Greece, not one, would have dreamed of — and yet I spurned them and chose you — a bride of hate to me, a bride of death — tigress, not woman, beast of wilder breath than Skylla shrieking over the Tuscan sea. Enough — no scorn of mine can reach you, the iron is so thick over your eyes. Out of my road, you crime-mother, blind with children's blood. Let me weep alone the bitter tide that washes Jason's days — no gentle bride to speak with anymore, no child to look upon whom once I raised. All — all gone forever.

MEDEA. I had an easy answer to all that swell of speech, but Zeus our father knows well what I did for you, and what you did for me. So let it lie. This was not to be — that you should live a merry life, my bed forgotten and my heart uncomforted — neither you nor your princess. Nor would the king who arranged your marriage drive Medea from his land and not suffer for it. Call me what you will: tigress, or Skylla from the Tuscan seas. My claws have gripped your heart, and everything is shining.
JASON. You also have grief. Your pain is as fierce as mine.
MEDEA. I love the pain — so long as you will laugh no more.
JASON. Oh, what a womb of sin my children came from.
MEDEA. Sons — did you die for your father's shame?
JASON. How? It was not my hand that murdered them.
MEDEA. It was your false wooings — your trampling pride.
JASON. You said it — for your lust for love they died.
MEDEA. And love to women should be a slight thing?
JASON. To pure women, yes. Your whole vile life to you.
MEDEA. Think of your torment — they are dead, they are dead.
JASON. No — quick, great God — quick curses around your head.
MEDEA. The Gods know who began this work of grief.
JASON. They know your heart and all its loathsomeness.
MEDEA. Loathe on. But oh — your voice — it hurts me sore.
JASON. And yours me. Would you hear me speak no more?
MEDEA. How? Show me the way — that is what I want.
JASON. Give me the dead to weep over and to bury. [She rises on the chariot and is slowly borne away.]

MEDEA. Never. I myself will lay them in a still green sepulchre, where Hera by the Hill has a holy precinct, so that no angry men can break their graves and cast them out to fresh evil. So I lay on this whole shore of Corinth a high feast forever and a rite, to purge them yearly of the stain of this poor blood. As for me, I go to the plain of Pallas, to live beside Pandion's son, Aegeus. For you — see — death is drawing on, evil and lonely, like your heart. The hands of your old Argo, rotting where she stands, shall smite your head in two — and bitter to the last shall be your memories of me.
JASON. May They who hear the weeping child blast you — and They who walk in blood.
MEDEA. Your broken vows — your beguiled friends — have shut the ears of God to you.
JASON. Go — you are wet with children's tears.
MEDEA. Go yourself — and lay your bride to sleep.
JASON. Childless, I go — to weep and weep.
MEDEA. Not yet — age is coming, and long years.
JASON. My sons — my own —
MEDEA. Not yours — mine.
JASON. — Who slew them.
MEDEA. Yes — to torture you.
JASON. Once let me kiss their lips — once put my arms around them — touch — Ah, woe is me.
MEDEA. Would you love them now and beg them? Just now they were nothing.
JASON. At the last, O God — to touch that tender forehead.
MEDEA. Your words are cast on the wind. [He casts himself upon the earth.]

JASON. You, Zeus, will hear me. All this is said for nothing. I am simply spurned aside, trampled by this tigress red with children's blood. Yet, come what may, as far as you have granted, as far as my strength may yet hold, I weep over these dead and say their last farewell, and raise my hand to all the powers of the air in witness of these things — how she who killed them will not let me gather up my babies and lay their bodies in the earth — whom, O stone of women, I wish I had never known, never fathered, only to have them slain by you.

CHORUS. Zeus has great treasuries in heaven, from which strange dooms come down on man, past hope and past fear. The end people looked for does not come, and a path opens where no one expected one. So has it fallen here.
